gapTheirs: Markers are set at the heading's own bold weight: one '#' carries 438 ink px vs B's 305 (+44%) while the 'H' glyph is identical (434 vs 432), so '######' at H6 reads as a solid picket fence competing with the word; the stair also misses its grid, stepping 26,26,25,26,25 px instead of a clean 26, with line pitch 74,73,73,73,73 instead of a flat 74.
verdict: The bones are the same in both - markers flush-right at x=194, every heading word landing on x=224, six rows, no wandering - so this comes down to whether the hash run knows its place. A's does not: it is bold, the same weight as the heading it labels, and by H6 you are reading a fence before you read the words, which is the exact failure this row exists to catch. B keeps the marks at the body's ink but drops the weight, so the stair reads as gutter and the words carry the line; that B's stair also steps an exact 26px each time while A's jitters 25/26 and its baselines drift off a 74px pitch just seals it. B's markers err light enough that counting #### against ##### is work, but that is a smaller sin than a heading you have to look past.

states.name: blocks
states.gap: A breaks weight mid-line at the H6 row: the `######` run is set regular (stems 3px at y=58) against 6px bold heading strokes, so the marker and the words it labels look like two different fonts on one line; and with ~25px-wide hashes on a 26px cell the six marks leave only a 1px gap and fuse into a single 155px hatch you cannot count at a glance.
states.gapTheirs: B sets the `######` run bold — hash stems 5–6px vs A's 3px, ink density 99.4 vs 75.5 mean grey over the identical 6-cell run (+32%) while the heading's own words are identically weighted in both (78.4 vs 77.5) — so the heaviest object on the whole screen is a six-hash slab hanging out at the container's left edge, louder than the sentence it labels. B also runs a fractional 25.6px cell (advances alternate 25/26/25/26/26px), landing the heading's `H` 2px left of the body column's `B` where A is 1px off.
states.verdict: These are the same page twice, and the argument is one weight step. B's six hashes hang out to the container edge in full bold and read as a black picket fence in the margin — your eye lands on the markup before the heading, which is exactly backwards for a screen you are supposed to write on. A keeps the run at text weight so the gutter stays texture and the bold words carry the heading, though A pays for it with a visible seam mid-line where 3px hashes meet 6px letters, and its hashes are packed so tight (1px between glyphs) that you count them by guess. Everything else — body column at x=225, `>`/`-`/`1.` sitting on it with no rule beside the quote, ~1.71 line-height — is a wash; A wins on the only row being judged.

states.name: wrapped
states.gap: Two cells of measure short of B: A's longest row reaches x=1637 in a 1750px frame (~113px right slack) against B's 1663 (~87px), so the wrapped block reads ~62 chars wide instead of 64 and every continuation row breaks one word earlier than the frame requires.
states.gapTheirs: Type set ~1.6% smaller — 25.6px advance vs A's 26.0px (em ~21.3 vs ~21.7 CSS px at 2x DPR) — and the two extra cells buy a raggier right edge: row-end ink swings 1459→1663 (204px, ~8 cells) vs A's 1482→1637 (155px, ~6 cells).
states.verdict: On the only row that decides this state — what a wrapped row does — these two are the same app: continuations hang in under the item's own first word at exactly 2 cells for `- ` and `> ` and 5 for `123. `, no ghost second `>`, no decorative rule. So the choice comes down to type, and A wins it by a hair: 26.0px advance against 25.6px, and a 6-cell rag against B's 8-cell rag, which is what you actually feel scanning four stacked continuation rows. B's answer to the same problem is to push two more characters per line and let the right edge flap; A leaves 26px on the table and keeps the column edge quieter. Nobody would notice the difference in a screenshot, and every writer would notice it by page forty.
